Oct 22 : Meta Platforms has a strong basis for arguing that the $25 billion penalty New Mexico secured this week in a case stemming from allegations the firm mishandled user data should be reduced on appeal, legal experts said.  The judgment was one of the largest state verdicts against a company in US history. It came after a jury found Meta misled consumers about who had access to their data in the wake of revelations that Cambridge Analytica, a political consulting firm involved in President Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, had harvested personal data from millions of Facebook users.  New Mexico said state law allowed for a penalty of up to $5,000 for each time someone in the state may have seen an allegedly misleading statement from Meta. Experts said the company would likely argue that Judge Francis Mathew should only have considered people who actually saw the statements.   "The most vulnerable basis on appeal is going to be the question about whether a violation is going to count, even in the absence of any proof that a particular person saw one of these misrepresentations or relied on them to their detriment," said Peter Ormerod, a law professor at Villanova University.

C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal. The company is expected to appeal the underlying jury verdict and the penalty. Meta has previously said that it does not sell user data and that New Mexico did not prove any consumer had actually been misled and that a penalty in the billions of dollars would risk violating its constitutional rights to due process and protection from excessive fines.  New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said on Wednesday he expected Meta to appeal the judgment and the state stood ready to defend its legal position. He did not immediately respond to a request for further comment. JURY FOUND 43 MILLION VIOLATIONS New Mexico's attorney general sued Meta in 2021, alleging that the company lied to Facebook users about who had access to their data, how the company handled hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform, and other internal policies.  Jurors on September 25 found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading. Multiplying those statements by their potential audience within New Mexico, the jury said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of the state’s consumer protection laws. The state had 1.4 million active Facebook users and a population of 2.1 million as of 2020.  Mathew said in his ruling on Wednesday that a penalty of more than $219 billion would be justified under state law, which allows a $5,000 penalty for each violation, but he reduced the amount. The state had urged Mathew to award the state between $35 billion and $40 billion, while Meta said penalties of no more than $3.45 billion were warranted.  Ormerod said that even if the company's appeals in state courts fail, Meta could argue to the US Supreme Court that the penalty violated its rights under the US Constitution to due process and against excessive fines.  The size of the penalty on its own does not mean it will be overturned, given the New Mexico law allowing for penalties for each willful violation, said Daryl Lim, a professor at Penn State Dickinson Law.  But it seems implausible that Meta was really responsible for so much financial harm, a sign the penalty may be unjust, said Eric Goldman, a professor at Santa Clara University School of Law. "It felt like there was a lot of duplicative counting in the calculations," Goldman said. "How many times can a single person be duped by the same entity?"

Source: Reuters

Oct 22 : Spotify forecast fourth-quarter profit above Wall Street estimates on Thursday, as the Swedish music streaming company bets on its AI-powered features to drive user growth in the crucial holiday season. The company expects operating income of €820 million ($920.53 million), compared with analysts' average estimate of €813.4 million, according to data compiled by LSEG. Shares of the company were last up more than 3 per cent in volatile premarket trading. Spotify offers AI-powered features such as its AI DJ, which curates personalized music mixes with spoken commentary, and prompt-based playlists that let users describe a mood or listening preference to generate tailored selections.

We've built a strong business that keeps compounding, we invest when we see a path for growth, our costs are moderating, and there is more runway ahead," co-CEO Alex Norstrom said in a statement. MANCHESTER, England, Oct 22 : Manchester City will try to preserve the Premier League's only perfect record at Aston Villa this weekend while dealing with mounting injuries and major off-field distractions following their guilty verdict on financial-rule charges. Enzo Maresca's City have won all seven league matches to sit three points clear of champions Arsenal, but an independent commission's finding that the club were guilty of 114 financial breaches has cast a shadow over their blistering start. City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed, with sanctions yet to be decided. Their immediate task is maintaining their flawless run at Villa Park on Saturday despite a growing injury list.

Forward Antoine Semenyo is set for a lengthy spell out with a knee injury, while wing back Nico O'Reilly and midfielders Mateo Kovacic and Matheus Nunes are doubts. League-leading scorer Erling Haaland was rested for Tuesday's 5-1 Champions League thrashing of AEK Athens because of a knock but is expected to be available against Villa. Arsenal, City's closest challengers on 18 points, host Everton on Saturday, although they have fitness concerns after Bukayo Saka limped off in the 10th minute of Wednesday's 2-2 Champions League draw at Bayern Munich with a quadriceps injury. "He doesn't look good at all, but we'll have to wait and see," Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta said. Fourth-placed Chelsea host London rivals Tottenham Hotspur at Stamford Bridge on Saturday after back-to-back league victories over Bournemouth and Everton. Spurs finally earned their first league victory of the season with Monday's 3-1 home win over Coventry City after a miserable start that has left them 16th with six points from seven games. Chelsea have 13 points. Liverpool face one of the tougher challenges of the weekend when they welcome high-flying Brighton & Hove Albion to Anfield on Sunday. Brighton's superb start has them third with five wins and a draw from seven matches, two places and four points above Liverpool, while their goal difference of plus 18 is the league's best. Liverpool, though, have uncovered another attacking weapon in 18-year-old Rio Ngumoha, who produced a dazzling performance in their 4-3 Champions League comeback win over Villarreal on Tuesday. Ngumoha created two goals and became the youngest Liverpool player to register a Champions League assist, earning a standing ovation from the Anfield crowd. "That's the good thing with Rio he is still 18, he is not the full package, he can add things fortunately for us. Hopefully he can continue in the same way," Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola said. "But I'm happy because attitude-wise I think he's in a great place." Liverpool's injury problems complicate the task, with the versatile Dominik Szoboszlai, wing back Jeremie Frimpong, right back Conor Bradley and striker Hugo Ekitike among those sidelined. At Old Trafford, Manchester United desperately need a victory over Bournemouth to breathe life into a season that has gone awry. Michael Carrick's team are 13th with one victory and seven points from their opening seven matches and are coming off a shambolic 4-1 Champions League defeat at Como on Wednesday. "I have to apologise to the supporters," Carrick said after the latest setback in Italy. "I care about this football club as much as anyone, if not more. "For us to play in that way, it's not acceptable. That bit of intensity, that aggression, that real willingness to give everything tonight was totally the opposite of the performance. It was tough to watch." Complicating matters, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo, Luke Shaw, Benjamin Sesko, Patrick Dorgu and Lisandro Martinez are among those with injury or fitness concerns, while midfielder Manuel Ugarte has a long-term knee injury. Carrick's United were held 1-1 at home by Tottenham and away to Leeds United in their last two league outings and now face a Bournemouth side who sit one point below them. For Manchester City, the challenge is almost the reverse. While their rivals search for momentum or try to keep pace, they head to Villa attempting to ensure the legal fight surrounding the club does not interrupt a perfect start on the pitch.

Source: Reuters

Oct 22 : Customers are increasingly asking where the AI inside their business software was built, SAP's finance chief told Reuters on Thursday, with export controls and Europe's sovereignty debate now shaping decisions once made on price and performance alone. "Could data used by that model be channelled out to end up in places where it shouldn't end up?" Dominik Asam said in the interview, describing a client question SAP regularly hears. It has become an art form to understand companies' precise requirements over technology governance when juggling several AI models, he added. SAP, Europe's most valuable tech company, embeds more than 70 models from various providers into its software that runs accounting and supply chains at many of the world's largest companies, a strategic choice to be agnostic on the market rather than internally build its own models. But for clients, where the AI comes from matters. A US customer may not accept components developed with Chinese models, while others' back-office work, including SAP's own, can run on open-weight software "from wherever it comes from", Asam said.

"If you're a Department of Defense of a large nation, you will think about that differently as opposed to a mom-and-pop shop." European debate over a possible "kill switch" in US cloud infrastructure has also fed the market for sovereign alternatives, Asam said. SAP has recently signed deals with governments and defence contractors, and prefers access to models from every region, including Europe and Canada, so it can offer a flexible portfolio to such clients, he said. Asked whether this week's PHP vulnerability disclosures had touched SAP, Asam said the company was using frontier AI models to attack and test its own products before anyone else could do it. "Anyone who says I don't have any vulnerabilities would lie to you," he said, while declining to comment on findings of such screenings.

FAST

JAKARTA: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto's big-tent coalition has given him almost unchecked power for two years, but mass food poisoning and graft linked to his flagship free meals programme have emerged as the first major test of their support for the former special forces commander. Two political parties in the coalition have already decided, after internal deliberations, to distance themselves from the programme, senior members from both parties with knowledge of the discussions told Reuters. A member of a third coalition party said their party feared the problems with the scheme would hurt their electoral prospects.  Together, the parties of the three people, who asked not to be identified because they feared repercussions for criticising Prabowo's policies, represent more than a quarter of his coalition's 80 per cent parliamentary majority, which includes seven of the eight parties in the house. Prabowo's Gerindra party has 15 per cent.  "Loyalty must also have limits," a member of one of the parties, which was once a vocal defender of the programme, told Reuters.

Prabowo made providing free, nutritious meals a cornerstone of his election campaign, promising to reach 83 million children and pregnant women, but several incidents of mass food poisoning, logistical challenges and allegations of corruption have left many Indonesians questioning the multibillion dollar initiative.  A poll conducted in early October by Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting (SMRC) showed about 62 per cent of the public opposed the programme, while approval for the president himself fell to the lowest since he took office. "What are the limits? The survival of our party," the party member said, adding internal polls showed the party's electability had fallen in July from January. They did not give further details of the confidential survey meant only for internal party consumption.

Related:

Indonesian officials say government-supplied meals tested after more than 500 students fall ill

Two years into presidency, Indonesia’s Prabowo faces tough balancing act between ambitious promises and fiscal discipline

"If by mid-2027 there are no improvements, the coalition will be fragile and things may eventually fall apart on their own," they said. Indonesia's next elections are due in early 2029. Until now, Prabowo - who marks two years in office this week - has faced little or no pushback. There have been no dissenting votes in parliament on any bills the government has proposed, not even by the one party that is not formally part of the ruling bloc. Nor has the leader of Southeast Asia's largest economy faced any speeches critical of his policies.  FALLING NUMBERS Tensions in Prabowo's coalition have risen as the president's approval rating has declined. Last November, the president had an 81 per cent rating, according to SMRC. That fell to 66.4 per cent in March, 51 per cent in July and 44.5 per cent in October. Positive opinions of the free meals programme have also slumped - from 62 per cent last November to just over a third in the most recent poll. In June, authorities arrested a former chief of the programme and two other officials on corruption charges. On Aug 31, dozens of families filed a police complaint against the government, marking the first legal action over the programme that started in January 2025. Early last month, about 1,700 people fell ill in four separate incidents after eating the meals, bringing the total number of cases of food poisoning to at least 57,000 since launch. The president's office and the National Nutrition Agency (NNA), which runs the initiative, did not respond to requests for comment. Sugiat Santoso, the Gerindra spokesperson, said the coalition remained strong and the programme was not intended to secure electoral gains.  "Every political party has its own targets and we respect that ... Whatever their stance, related to free meals or not, supporting Prabowo or not, we respect it," Sugiat said, adding that the NNA was working to improve the programme.

Students rest while receiving treatment for food poisoning at the regional general hospital after eating government-sponsored free school meals in Pati, Central Java province, Indonesia, on Sep 9, 2026. (File photo: Reuters/Ragil Kuswanto)

The National Mandate Party, one of the six parties in Prabowo's coalition, said it remained committed to supporting the programme. Any shortcomings should be addressed "systematically and collectively," said Viva Yoga Mauladi, its deputy chief.  The other parties did not respond to Reuters requests for comment.  SYMPATHY FOR VICTIMS A senior member in a second coalition party said an increasing number of voters were complaining about the programme.  The party has asked its lawmakers to start "constructive public criticism" of the scheme using "polite language," the person said.  Both parties where the senior members said they planned to express their concerns publicly, said they also aimed to push the government to improve the programme. Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka recently publicly apologised for the food poisoning cases, visiting some of the affected children. Gibran is the son of Joko Widodo, who defeated Prabowo in the 2014 and 2019 presidential elections, and whose backing was key to Prabowo finally winning the presidency in 2024.    Prabowo, meanwhile, has publicly defended the initiative. In February, he played down the food poisoning incidents, saying the number of cases was statistically insignificant. "99.99 per cent of the programme can be considered successful,” he said.

Related:

New head of Indonesia’s free meals programme quits after 45 days citing health reasons, as budget cuts loom

Some remote Indonesian communities still await free meals as programme resumes after review

In August, Prabowo pledged improvements. "I am determined to continue the free nutritious programme but with improvements and efficiency," he said. "MAJOR BLOW" The free meals programme has created broader political pressure on coalition parties with ministers from those parties facing criticism and attacks on social media when speaking about it, said Burhanuddin Muhtadi, a senior visiting fellow at Singapore's Yusof Ishak Institute.  If the scheme failed, it would be a "major blow" for the president given it was central to the 2024 election campaign, he added.  "Prabowo could revise his policy by making the programme more targeted, so it would be more feasible to manage and would not incur such high budget. However, it appears he has not significantly changed the universal design, proven by the programme's very large budget allocation next year," Burhanuddin said. The government has budgeted 240 trillion rupiah for the scheme next year. The problems with the free meals programme are unfolding as the president faces economic challenges from the cost of living to MSCI's warning that it could exclude Indonesia from its stock market indices, potentially cutting it off from international capital. "Prabowo must demonstrate commitment and integrity, not only making statements," said Mohammad Ezha Fachriza Roshady, SMRC's researcher.

Source: Reuters/lk

MELBOURNE, Oct 22 : Emotions are running high ahead of MotoGP's final Australian Grand Prix at Phillip Island on Sunday, with riders to bid a reluctant farewell to one of the championship's most beloved circuits before the race moves to the streets of Adelaide. Barring two years lost to the COVID-19 pandemic, the seaside track south of Melbourne has been a fixture on the world championship calendar for 30 years and produced some of Australian motorcycling's most memorable moments. Australian twice world champion Casey Stoner celebrated six wins in succession from 2007 to 2012, while compatriot Mick Doohan sealed his fifth and final world title with victory in the 1998 race.  Both riders have sections of the track named after them, along with the country's first premier class world champion Wayne Gardner, who won back-to-back in 1989-90 in the grand prix's first two races in the global series.

The island's combination of high-speed corners and fickle weather has often produced drama, and millions of fans have attended race weekends over the decades. Hundreds of local residents gathered at roadsides on Thursday to greet the racers as they crossed San Remo bridge to the island on a processional ride to the track. "Phillip Island is an extraordinary circuit. Racing here for the last time will be emotional,” said Ducati’s Marc Marquez, who has won five races at the circuit including four MotoGP events. “It is a track with a unique, breathtaking layout." ADELAIDE STREET CIRCUIT However, it is also a far-flung track with ageing facilities long overdue for an upgrade. With the 2026 race marking the end of a long-term contract with the Victorian state government, MotoGP organisers Dorna pushed to move the grand prix to Albert Park, which hosts a Formula One race in central Melbourne in the autumn. With the two sides failing to reach agreement on renewing the contract, the South Australian government stepped in to cut a deal with Dorna and will host the race in Adelaide on MotoGP's first street circuit in 2027. Stoner said local organisers had not tried hard enough to keep the race at Phillip Island or build a festival atmosphere around it as seen every year at the buzzing F1 grand prix. "I think it’s a lot to do with the Victorian government that’s dropped the ball with it and maybe they wanted to, I’m not sure," he told Melbourne's Herald Sun newspaper. The Victorian government said in a statement it had declined Dorna's request to move the race to Albert Park. Aprilia rider Jorge Martin leads the championship by two points from Ducati's Marquez. Last year's winner Raul Fernandez said he would "cry a little" on the final weekend at Phillip Island. "Not because I got my first MotoGP victory here but also because I always enjoy it a lot coming here to Phillip Island - it is super nice," the Trackhouse rider said in quotes published by motor racing website Crash.net. “It's a track that everybody will miss a little bit.” After a week of sunshine at the island, rain is forecast for qualifying on Saturday, and a storm may even disrupt Sunday's race. Home racer Jack Miller, a decent performer in the wet, was not complaining ahead of his final Australian Grand Prix. "Phillip Island's giving itself a proper send-off," he told reporters at the circuit on Thursday. "I'm not angry about that."

Source: Reuters

SEOUL, Oct 22 : South Korea's Samsung Electro-Mechanics will receive investment valued at 3.7 trillion won ($2.8 billion) from Tesla and Nvidia to build facilities making advanced chip substrates, known as FC-BGA for AI semiconductors, the Maeil Business Newspapera reported on Thursday. Tesla will invest 1.1 trillion won and Nvidia 2.6 trillion won to build the production lines in the South Korean city of Sejong to supply the substrates under a long-term contract, the paper reported, citing industry sources.
